Guideline Statement
Exhibition Place is committed to supporting people with disabilities by working to remove
existing barriers and ensuring that new barriers are not created.
Application
Legislation has been passed, including the Ontario Human Rights Code, Ontarians with
Disabilities Act, 2001, and the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005, and its
regulations, and Exhibition Place is committed to meeting its obligations under the
legislation.
These pieces of legislation include either implied or express accessibility obligations that
apply to the acquisition of all goods and services, including those goods and services that
may be acquired regardless of value.
Implementation
In order to meet their accessibility obligations in procurement related activities, Divisions
should consider the following three key questions:
     • What are the barriers that people with disabilities might face in trying to use the
       goods, services, or facilities you are planning to acquire?
   • Will these goods, services, or facilities be used by members of the public or by
       Exhibition Place employees?
   • What are the appropriate accessibility criteria and how can they be incorporated into
       the procurement process?
The following steps should assist you in answering these questions:
     •    Step 1: Review the definitions of ‘disability’ and ‘barrier’.
     •    Step 2: Conduct an assessment to determine whether these types of goods or
          services could create barriers for people with disabilities, and whether they are
          members of the public or Exhibition Place employees.
     •    Step 3: Include accessibility considerations in your procurement business case.
     •    Step 4: Develop the related procurement documents, and include relevant
          accessibility specifications based on the barriers identified.
     •    Step 5: Document and retain information relating to your compliance with
          accessibility obligations.
     •    Step 6: Ensure that the successful vendor meets their accessibility obligations
          throughout the term of the contract.




Accessibility Obligations in Procurement Guidelines                                            Page 1 of 5
 Step 1: Review the definitions of ‘disability’ and ‘barrier’.
As defined in the Ontario Human Rights Code, Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2001, and the
Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005.
Disability means:
     • Any degree of physical disability, infirmity, malformation or disfigurement that is
       caused by bodily injury, birth defect, and illness, and without limiting the generality of
       the foregoing includes: diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, brain injury, any degree of
       paralysis, amputation, lack of physical co-ordination, blindness or visual impediment,
       deafness or hearing impediment, muteness or speech impediment, physical reliance
       on a guide dog or other animal, and a wheelchair or other remedial appliance or
       device.
    • A condition of mental impairment or a developmental disability.
    • A learning disability or dysfunction in one or more of the processes involved in
       understanding, using symbols, and spoken language.
    • A mental disorder.
       An injury or disability for which benefits were claimed or received under the
       insurance plan established under the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997;
       (‘handicap’). As defined in the Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2001, and the
       Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005.
Barrier means:
Anything that prevents a person with a disability from fully participating in all aspects of
society because of his or her disability including: physical barrier, architectural barrier,
information or communications barrier, attitudinal barrier, technological barrier, policy,
and practice.
Step 2: Conduct an assessment to determine whether these types of goods or
services could create barriers for people with disabilities, and whether they are
members of the public or Exhibition Place employees.
In order to ensure that the goods, services, and facilities you intend to procure will deliver
the desired benefits to all potential users, determine whether it could create barriers for
people with disabilities. The Ministry of Community and Social Services ‘Understanding
Barriers to Accessibility’ document might help you identify existing and potential barriers
that you might not have considered.
Procurement of goods or services for members of the public.
If members of the public will be making use of the goods, services, and facilities you are
planning to acquire, it is likely that many of them will be people with disabilities.
Currently, 15.5% of the population are people with disabilities, and this number is likely to
grow to 20% in the next few years with the aging of our population.
Goods, services, and facilities that will be used by the public will require that accessibility
features be integrated into their design and implementation to ensure that people with
disabilities can make use of them.




Accessibility Obligations in Procurement Guidelines                                      Page 2 of 5
 For example: In acquiring or deploying public access kiosks and point of sale devices, the
ability of a person in a wheelchair or scooter to use the services could be limited if the
keypad is not situated properly. If the keypad buttons are not in Braille or if the terminal only
includes touch-screen technology, a person with a visual impairment would not be able to
access the services provided.
When installing washroom facilities, assess whether a person who uses personal support
services (e.g. attendant services) would be able to use the washroom comfortably with his
or her attendant in a unisex or family washroom.
As set out in the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005, Accessibility
Standards for Customer Service Regulation, customers with disabilities must be
accommodated when providing them with goods and services. When acquiring services for
the public from an external provider, the procurement document should specify that the
vendor needs to ensure that its staff are trained in customer service for people with
disabilities, and are able to interact and deliver these services appropriately.
Procurement of goods or services for Exhibition Place employees
In addition, Exhibition Place employees with disabilities may need to be accommodated in
the workplace and in the provision of goods and services. Exhibition Place employees may
require specific accommodations to ensure that they are able to carry out their work without
encountering barriers. This may include the procurement of accessible workspaces,
equipment modifications, provision of assistive devices, and access to touch or voice
activated equipment. Meeting accessibility obligations for goods and services requires
specifications that include options for various types of disabilities, and are open to individual
accommodation needs.
For example: When purchasing or installing a photocopier, you should assess whether the
display screen and function keys may need to be used by a person who is blind or has low
vision, and determine whether the height of the photocopier can easily be reached by
someone using a wheelchair or scooter.
When purchasing telephones, you might want to assess whether the equipment requires
volume controls, clear display screens, and large buttons in order to make the telephones
as accessible to as many users as possible.
Procuring accessible goods, services, and facilities is usually more economical than
restructuring the goods, services, or facilities to meet accessibility criteria afterward.
Step 3: Include accessibility considerations in your procurement business case.
The level of detail in your business case may vary, based on the nature of the acquisition.
You may wish to include a description of the need to provide accessible goods or services
currently and in the future.
For example: When acquiring the services of a facilitator or consultant to conduct a public
meeting, ensure that the location for the meeting is wheelchair accessible. Consider
whether sign language interpretation, alternate format materials, and other accommodations
are required to enable the full participation of all attendees.




Accessibility Obligations in Procurement Guidelines                                     Page 3 of 5
 When acquiring computers or other desktop equipment, consider whether the system has
the capacity for adaptive technology upgrades such as speech reading, voice activated
software, and large fonts.
Consulting with community agencies that provide services for people with disabilities may
give you information on accessibility needs, which may be helpful in planning services and
accommodations. Keep in mind however, that individuals often have unique
accommodation needs, which can best be determined by consulting with them directly.
Market research may help you determine the capability of vendors to provide accessible
goods and services to people with disabilities, and confirm the nature of the accessibility
specifications and requirements that should be included in procurement documents. Gather
information from health and safety associations on the type and availability of suppliers, to
provide ergonomic goods and services to support decisions about procuring office related
equipment universally accessible to a broad range of people. An analysis of possible
procurement strategies and options for acquiring and deploying accessible goods or
services including the associated cost/benefit analysis.
For example: Reviewing the different approaches for communicating with individuals who
are deaf, hard of hearing, and who have speech impairments could help support a
purchasing decision. You may wish to consider whether it would be appropriate to purchase
a single TTY for an entire division, or invest in TTY software that would enable a large
number of TTY users to communicate directly to staff through their computers.
If you determine that it is not practicable to incorporate accessibility criteria and features in
your procurement, you may be asked to provide an explanation. You may wish to include
this explanation in your business case.
Step 4: Develop the related procurement documents and include relevant
accessibility specifications based on the barriers identified.
The specifications in the procurement document should clearly articulate and include all the
accessibility requirements for immediate acquisitions, or provide for the acquisition of
goods and services to meet accessibility requirements should you determine that
accessible goods or services would be needed in the future.
The procurement document should provide detailed specifications including accessibility
criteria and features, based on the identified needs.
For example: The specifications for the provision of customer services could require a
vendor to complete training programs on accessibility, diversity, and inclusion before or
shortly after being hired to complete the contract.
The specifications in producing a public report could require a vendor to produce the report
in a different print colour, font style and size, as well as, in alternate formats such as html,
word, large print, Braille, audio CDs/DVDs, accessible PDFs, and require captioning, text,
and/or ASL for videos.
When incorporating accessibility criteria and features into your procurement documents you
may wish to consider sample accessibility language taken from the reference material
Accessibility Language for Procurement Documents.



Accessibility Obligations in Procurement Guidelines                                     Page 4 of 5
 Ensure that your procurement document is posted in an accessible format, and includes a
contact email address and phone number for requests for alternate formats.
Step 5: Document and retain information relating to your compliance with
accessibility obligations.
You must document and retain information relating to compliance with the Ontarians with
Disabilities Act, 2001, and the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005, and its
regulations where applicable.
If you did not incorporate accessibility criteria and features in your procurement, you may be
asked to provide an explanation, which must be provided in an accessible format or with
appropriate communications supports.
Any accessibility related feedback from people with disabilities should be kept on file for
reference to improve the accessibility of future procurements.
Step 6: Ensure that the successful vendor meets their accessibility obligations
throughout the term of the contract.
Engaging in active contract management will enable you to monitor and manage the
successful vendor's performance, and ensure compliance with the terms of the contract
including accessibility obligations. Your contract management framework may include
conducting periodic site visits, performance audits, and soliciting client feedback as
appropriate. It may be helpful to document lessons learned to use in subsequent
procurement initiatives.

Policy Statement
The Board of Governors of Exhibition Place is committed to building an inclusive
organization that values the contributions of people with disabilities, and to providing an
accessible environment in which people with disabilities can access Exhibition Place’s
goods, services, and facilities, including buildings, public spaces, information and
communications, in a way that meets their individual needs. Exhibition Place is committed to
the identification, removal, and prevention of accessibility barriers, including attitudinal,
systemic, information, communications, technology, and built environment and physical
barriers.
This Policy establishes an overarching framework for compliance with the commitment of
Exhibition Place to accessibility, including the requirements of the Accessibility for
Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005 (AODA) and the Integrated Accessibility Standards
Regulation (IASR).
The AODA is a structure that provides for the development, implementation, and
enforcement of accessibility standards in order to achieve accessibility for persons with
disabilities. All Exhibition Place policies, procedures, bylaws, standards, and guidelines
must comply with legislation and provide for dignity, independence, integration, and equal
opportunity for people with disabilities. As required by the AODA, Exhibition Place must:
     •    Identify, prevent, and remove barriers people with disabilities face in accessing
          Exhibition Place’s goods, services, and facilities.
     •    Accommodate the accessibility needs of people with disabilities to ensure they
          obtain, use, or benefit from Exhibition Place goods, services, and facilities, and that
          they can do so in a timely manner, at a cost no greater than the cost for people
          without disabilities.
     •    Develop and train Exhibition Place employees on providing accessible goods,
          services, and facilities.
Application
General Application
This policy applies to all employees and volunteers.
Any individual or third party organization that provides goods, services, and facilities to the
public on behalf of Exhibition Place is also required to demonstrate compliance with this
Policy, including training as described in the General Requirements Training section.
The Employment Standards Requirements apply only to employees of Exhibition Place.
Roles & Responsibilities
Accessibility is a shared responsibility and everyone has a part to play in making Exhibition
Place accessible to residents, visitors, attendees, and co-workers as follows:


Accessibility Policy                                                                    Page 1 of 13
 1. Employees, Volunteers, and Third Parties
All employees and other persons acting on behalf of Exhibition Place are expected to:
     • have thorough knowledge of and maintain compliance with this Policy
     • be familiar with their rights and responsibilities under this Policy
     • prevent accessibility barriers by including accessibility considerations in the
       development of goods, services, and facilities
    • participate in identifying accessibility barriers and planning for barrier removal
    • provide a welcoming environment for people with disabilities, including any person
       with a disability using assistive devices, and accompanied by a support person or
       service animal
    • provide information and communications in accessible formats upon request with
       communication supports, and consulting with the requestor about their preferred
       format
    • facilitate the process of receiving and responding to feedback about the manner that
       Exhibition Place provides goods, services, and facilities to persons with disabilities,
       and ensure all feedback processes are accessible to persons with disabilities by
       providing and arranging for accessible formats and communication supports upon
       requests
    • facilitate requests for accommodation by members of the public and employees with
       disabilities in a timely manner, to the point of undue hardship in accordance with the
       Ontario Human Rights Code and the Exhibition Place Accommodation Policy
    • when serving customers that have competing accommodation needs, staff will make
       every effort to meet the needs of all individuals according to the Ontario Human
       Rights Code and Exhibition Place’s Accommodation Policy
    • request support from supervisors, managers, directors, and senior management
       when accommodation requests are outside their area of responsibility or beyond their
       capacity
    • attend mandatory training and any additional training appropriate to the duties of
       their role, which may include acquiring skills and competencies necessary to identify,
       prevent, and remove accessibility barriers.
2. Directors, Managers, and Supervisors
In addition to the roles and responsibilities of the Policy, individuals with management and
supervisory roles are expected to:
     •    provide leadership in building an inclusive and accessible environment for the public
          and employees
     •    prevent barriers by including accessibility considerations in the development of new
          policies, practices, procedures, and bylaws
     •    ensure the Policy is communicated to all Exhibition Place employees and those
          acting on behalf of Exhibition Place
     •    promote awareness of the Policy within their area of responsibility
     •    monitor current practices and ensure that management and staff are held
          accountable for their responsibilities under this Policy
     •    act on non-compliant issues within their area of responsibility

       behalf of Exhibition Place have been provided with training, either by Exhibition
       Place or their own organization, as described in the General Requirements Training
       section and the Employment Standards Requirements section.
    • facilitate requests for accommodation by members of the public and employees with
       disabilities in a timely manner, to the point of undue hardship, in accordance with the
       Ontario Human Rights Code and the Exhibition Place Accommodation Policy
    • consult with the Senior Management Team for assistance with accessibility issues
3. Senior Management Team
In addition to roles and responsibilities of this Policy, individual senior management team
members must:
     • ensure resources are budgeted for identifying and preventing accessibility barriers
       (including attitudinal, systemic, information, communications and technology, and
       built environment and public space barriers), and for planning barrier removal
   • provide oversight for implementation of this Policy and compliance with the AODA
       within area of responsibility
   • provide accessibility compliance assurance when required
The Chief Executive Officer is responsible for promoting awareness of the Policy and for
reporting compliance to the Province in accordance with the AODA reporting deadlines.
The Chief Executive Officer is responsible for preparing an annual report to the Board of
Governors on the implementation of this Policy.
4. Exhibition Place AODA Implementation Team
The Exhibition Place AODA Implementation Team made up of senior management shall:
     •develop internal expertise and familiarity with the rights and responsibilities under
      this Policy
   • develop an implementation plan related to the Multi-Year Accessibility Plan
   • make recommendations to the Chief Executive Officer on the implementation of the
      Multi-Year Accessibility Plan and this Policy
5. The Board of Governors of Exhibition Place
The Board shall:
     •    approve of any revisions to the Accessibility Policy
     •    approve the Multi-Year Accessibility Plan
     •    approve an annual report, or more frequent if required, detailing the implementation
          of the Multi-Year Accessibility Plan.
Definitions
Accessibility
A concept integral to human rights that refers to the absence of barriers that prevent
individuals and groups from fully participating in all social, economic, political, and cultural

Accessibility Policy                                                                   Page 3 of 13
 aspects of society. The term is often linked to people with disabilities and their rights to
access, and also refers to design characteristics of products, devices, information, services,
facilities, and public spaces that enable independent use or support when required, and
access by people with a variety of disabilities.
Refers to products, devices, information, services, facilities, or public spaces that provide
for independent, equitable, and dignified access for people with disabilities, including but
not limited to those with visual, auditory, sensory, cognitive, and mobility related disabilities.
The concept of accessible design ensures both ‘direct access’ (i.e. unassisted) and ‘indirect
access’ referring to compatibility with a person's assistive technology.
Accessible Formats
Refers to formats that are usable by persons with disabilities including but not limited to:
large print, recorded audio, electronic formats, and Braille.
Accommodation
In the context of Human Rights, accommodation means preventing and removing barriers
caused by attitudinal, systemic, physical, information, communications, and technology
barriers that unfairly exclude individuals or groups protected by Ontario’s Human Rights
Code from having equal access to full benefits available to others.
Principles of accommodation include dignity, individualization, inclusion and integration. For
more information refer to Ontario's Human Rights Code and Exhibition Place's
Accommodation Policy.
Assistive Devices
Refers to technical aids, communication devices, medical aids modified or customized for
use to increase, maintain, or improve the functional ability of a person with a disability
including but not limited to wheelchairs, walkers, white canes, note taking devices, portable
magnifiers, recording machines, assistive listening devices, personal oxygen tanks, and
devices for grasping. Assistive devices may accompany the customer or already be on the
premises for the purpose of assisting persons with disabilities in carrying out activities or in
accessing the services provided by Exhibition Place.
Barrier
Defined by the AODA as anything that prevents a person with a disability from fully
participating in all aspects of society because of his or her disability, including a physical
barrier, architectural barrier, information or communications barrier, attitudinal barrier, a
technological barrier, and a policy or practice.
Career Development and Advancement
Defined by the AODA as the provision of additional responsibility within an employee’s
current position or movement from one job to another within the organization that may be
higher in pay, provide greater responsibility, or be at a higher level in the organization.
Communications
Refers to interaction between two or more persons or entities, or any combination of them
where information is provided, sent, and received.


Accessibility Policy                                                                   Page 4 of 13
 Communications Supports
Includes, but is not limited to, captioning, alternative and augmentative communications
supports, plain language, sign language, and other supports that facilitate effective
communications.
Disability
‘Disability’ is defined, per Section 2 of the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act,
2005, S.O. 2005, c. 11 and the Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, as
follows:
     •    any degree of physical disability, infirmity, malformation or disfigurement that is
          caused by bodily injury, birth defect or illness and, without limiting the generality of
          the foregoing, includes diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, a brain injury, any degree of
          paralysis, amputation, lack of physical co-ordination, blindness or visual impediment,
          deafness or hearing impediment, muteness or speech impediment, and physical
          reliance on a guide dog or other animal, wheelchair, and other remedial appliance or
          device
     •    a condition of mental impairment or a developmental disability, a learning disability,
          and a dysfunction in one or more of the processes involved in understanding or using
          symbols or spoken language
     •    a mental disorder, injury, or disability for which benefits were claimed or received
          under the insurance plan established under the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act,
          1997
Goods, Services, and Facilities
All aspects of Exhibition Place as an employer and service provider, including delivery of
goods, services, programs, all information and communication including verbal, print, audio,
video, websites, web application, and web content, and other digital technologies including
kiosks, all buildings, facilities, public spaces, and the public realm.
Information
Includes but is not limited to data, facts, and knowledge that exists in any format, including
text, audio, digital, or images that convey meaning.
Kiosk
Refers to an interactive electronic terminal including a point-of-sale device intended for
public use that allows users to access one or more services or products or both.
New Internet Website
Refers to either a website with a new domain name or a website with an existing domain
name undergoing a significant refresh.
Performance Management
Defined by the AODA as a program that defines and assesses employee performance,
productivity, and effectiveness, with the goal of facilitating employee success.

 Practicable

accessibility is practicable may include:
     •    Availability of accessible services, goods including commercial software or tools, or

     •    Technological compatibility between older products and newer ones being procured
Public Spaces
Refers to outdoor recreational trails, beach access routes, boardwalks, ramps, outdoor
public use eating areas, outdoor play spaces, outdoor paths of travel, accessible parking,
and service counters.
Redeployment
Refers to signing an employee to another job, department, and division within the
organization as an alternative to layoff, when a particular job, department, and division within
the organization has been downsized or eliminated.

COMMENTS
Through the Financial System Transformation Program, the City of Toronto (City) is
responding to the enterprise need to undergo a financial transformation, enabled by
modern technologies that will meet current and future business needs. This includes
standardizing finance processes, modernizing the finance service operating model, and
streamlining the underlying financial platform to ensure consistent access to timely
financial information in an efficient and effective system.
Fully embracing the scope of transformation contemplated by FSTP will require the City
to change the structure and way that its enterprise-wide finance function operates. The
requested funds will allow the City to complete the design of the Target Operating
Model (TOM) to a sufficiently detailed level, socialize the refined TOM with leadership
stakeholders, update the FSTP benefits case, and prepare a roadmap and plan to
enable the implementation of the new enterprise-wide Finance TOM in alignment with
the overall FSTP timelines. This work is anticipated to span a period of approximately
six months, starting in July/Aug 2022 through to November/December 2022.
The award of contract to Ernst & Young LLP for Active Risk Management Advisory
Services for FSTP is in accordance with current implementation best practice. The

To:           Board of Management

From:         Robin D. Hale
              Chief Operating Officer

Subject:      ATTENDANCE AND REVENUE REPORT - DECEMBER 2015

Date:         2016-02-17

Summary:

This report will update the Board of Management on the visitor statistics and revenue results for
the year ended 2015-12-31. Included in this report is a dashboard highlighting some of the key
metrics.

Recommendations:

It is recommended that the report be received for information.

Background:

In accordance with Zoo By-law No. 2-2010, attendance and revenues are reported to the Board on
a monthly basis. The budgeted monthly allocation of the attendance target is based upon rolling
five-year averages by month and accumulated year-to-date. The targets also reflect any shifts in
the calendar for statutory holidays and number of weekends each month.

Comments/Discussions:

In the early part of 2015, extreme cold weather had a significant influence on results with a total
of thirty-nine (39) extreme cold weather alerts issued in in the first quarter of the year. This
impacted 43.3% of the days in the first three months and in fact, the month of February was the
coldest month ever on record. This ultimately presented a key challenge related to Zoo
attendance as it proved very difficult to recover given the 2015 budget target. The corresponding
impact on revenue performance was mitigated somewhat in the area of parking operations, with
the benefits of revenue resulting from the effect of the price increase.

The Zoo participated with much enthusiasm in the build up to the highly anticipated 2015 Pan
Am Games by hosting torch bearer, Max Domi, during the relay. Although the 2015 Pan Am
Games had a number of success stories, they did not have the influence on attendance that was
anticipated. The effect of traffic congestion and warnings to avoid using highways where
necessary, appeared to negatively impact the decision of many visitors related to a trip by car to
the Zoo in the summer months.
 Attendance and Revenue Report – December 2015
2016-02-17
Page 2 of 3

Efforts to stimulate attendance continued throughout the fall season with a busy schedule of events at
the Zoo. The success of these efforts was evidenced by a lift in Q4 attendance of 7.2% versus the
same period in 2014 and a reduction of 2.4% in the budget variance versus Q3 2015.

The discounted admission offer using Groupon launched in late September was quite successful with
a total of 19,645 redemptions through the end of the offer period on December 31st, representing
74.6% of the 26,341 admission purchases through the duration of the Groupon offering.

Other key fall activities focused on stimulating interest in the Zoo included more than 4,000 people
participating in the 2015 Oasis Zoo Run; over 1,200 seniors attending on Senior’s Day; a Field Trip
Preview Weekend Event for Educators; serving as a host venue for CIBC Run for the Cure
Walk/Run in Scarborough; Member appreciation events in October; Red Panda and World Rhino
animal awareness days to bring further attention to the work done to save and protect species at the
Toronto Zoo and abroad; festive visits from Santa and the annual Boxing Day Treats Walk.

The birth of white lion cubs in late September and their introduction to the public in mid-
December resulted in positive interest in the Toronto Zoo. Together with the birth of the giant
panda cubs in early October and the polar bear cub in November, by the end of December 2015
these “babies” had reached over 8,970,434 people through various social media channels. It is
anticipated that this will assist in positively impacting attendance once they have all been
introduced to the public in the January – March timeframe of 2016.

As outlined in Schedule I, full year attendance for 2015 totaled 1,141,162 visitors for the year.
Although this impacted the visitor facing revenue streams, the attendance and revenue
enhancement program in the latter part of the year assisted in mitigating the impact of the
attendance trend and, in combination with cost containment measures, reduced the impact on the
net expenditure results versus the budget target. Regardless of the difficulties related to achieving
the attendance target in 2015, throughout the period of time supported by the Giant Panda
experience, it remains notable that the Toronto Zoo has seen more than 3.79 million visitors come
through the gates and over $97.3 million in visitor facing revenues. As a result, once the accounts
are finalized for 2015, the Zoo is still anticipating over $1.0 million remaining in the Zoo
Stabilization Reserve.

For your information, the full year results for attendance and primary revenue categories in 2015
are outlined in the tables and charts included in Schedule I.

the amount of $1,588,846.00 which includes a cash allowance of $10,000.00 and

FINANCIAL IMPACT

The financing for this project is included within the City approved Exhibition Place 2024

COMMENTS

Background

Most of the existing exterior lighting throughout Exhibition Place use obsolete
components, which requires extensive work to maintain, and overdue for replacement.
In 2023, a lighting assessment was completed which identified numerous opportunities
to improve lighting in general and light levels. Light levels in many areas are not
sufficient for safety and security, providing adequate lighting in public areas will create a
safe and inviting environment for guests and the general public.

The Lighting Study had also recommended replacement and addition of façade lighting
for the Horse Palace and Coliseum Complex to accent the architectural features. This
project also incorporates the renewal of façade lighting with the intention of highlighting
the historic significance.

The advances in technology of LED lighting make it attractive to replace current metal
halide, high pressure sodium and fluorescent lighting with LED lighting systems. LED
lighting is about 40% more energy efficient when compared with metal halide, high
pressure sodium and fluorescent fixtures. In addition, the Government of Canada's
Department of the Environment has proposed amendments to the regulations for
products containing mercury, which will phase out the use of these lamps within the
next few years.

Tender Process

The tender for this contract was issued on April 18, 2024 through the Exhibition Place
Purchasing and Materials Stores via Bonfire Online Procurement System and closed on
May 10, 2024. Ten (10) bidders attended the mandatory site tour meeting, and three (3)
submissions were received, all of which were compliant with the tender requirements.
The bidders' price submissions, excluding HST, are as shown in the following Table 1:

Table 1: Tender Price Submission and the Recommended Contract
                                         Bid Price       Additional       Recommended
 Bidder
                                         Received        Prices           Contract Price

 Kudlak-Baird (1982) Limited             $1,449,773.58   $461,781.00
 Rogol Electric Company Limited          $1,748,200.00   $545,000.00

Staff have reviewed the bids and based on its safety record and experience with similar
projects staff recommends award of the contract to the lowest compliant bidder, CMS
Electrical Group Ltd.
Lighting Upgrades on Exhibition Place Grounds                                      Page 2 of 3
 The additional prices included are for the following items in Appendix II of the bid
documents:
• Better Living Centre: Replace existing HID cluster pole fixtures (approx. 5 fixtures
   per pole) with LED globe lights to match existing style.
• South Pathway (from Ontario Drive to New Brunswick Way) Option 1: Replace
   existing “flagpoles” lighting fixture and pole with new LED fixture and pole. Reuse
   existing concrete base and conduit/wiring.
• Coca Cola Coliseum Facade lighting on Manitoba Drive: Install LED flood light
   fixtures on existing concrete light poles along Manitoba Drive comes with colour
   changing capabilities and DMX control and accessories. Include all underground
   infrastructure and provide communications wiring to suit. Replace existing HID wall
   pack fixtures with LED fixtures for Coca-Cola Coliseum North Facade. New DMX
   controllers to be located in the closest Electrical Room in West Annex

The recommended construction price of $1,588,846.00 will be funded from the
approved 2024 State of Good Repair Capital Budget.

CMS has approximately 160 employees and has completed several similar lighting
projects in the past three years for clients such as WPP, Canada Goose, and Wave,
meeting all tender requirements including those of qualification and experience. CMS
has also recently completed the various buildings lighting project at Exhibition Place and
are also currently working on the relocation and upgrade of IT rooms at the Enercare
Centre project. The consultant Studio TLA has reviewed the bid prices and has also
recommended to proceed with an award to CMS.

This recommendation is contingent upon approval by the Office of the City CFO &
Treasurer and of the Surety Company proposed by the successful bidder for the supply
of the bonding requirements. It is also subject to the City Fair Wage Office confirming
that the recommended contractor and its subcontractors maintain wage rates and
working conditions in accordance with Toronto Workers’ Rights requirements.

                  Open Meeting Requirements

• As a City Board the Toronto Zoo Board of Management is governed by the
  open meeting rules of the City of Toronto Act, 2006.

• Under the Act, the public is entitled to attend meetings of the Board, except
  when the meeting is properly closed for a small number of subjects.

• An investigation or court may find an informal gathering of members
  constitutes a meeting (e.g. a quorum is present; the discussion advances the
  business of the board).

  Zoo Board of Management and other City Boards.

    Codes of Conduct for Citizen Board Members

• When acting in her or his capacity as a member of a City agency or
  corporation board, the Member is bound by provisions of the Code of
  Conduct for Members of Local Boards (Restricted Definition) that are specific
  to the requirements of that board.

• The Code is similar to the Code of Conduct which applies to City Councillors.

• This Code of Conduct is accompanied by a procedural document called the
  Complaints Protocol .

• Board Members are bound by the Code of Conduct and should become
  familiar with its key elements governing personal conduct.

                  Code of Conduct Principles
• Members of local boards shall serve and be seen to serve the City and
  community in a conscientious and diligent manner.

• Members of local boards should be committed to performing their functions
  with integrity and to avoiding the improper use of the influence of their
  office, and conflicts of interest, both apparent and real.

• Members of local boards are expected to perform their duties in office and
  arrange their private affairs in a manner that promotes public confidence
  and will bear close public scrutiny.

• Members of local boards shall seek to serve the City’s and the public’s
  interest by upholding both the letter and the spirit of applicable laws of the
  Federal Parliament and Ontario Legislature, and the laws and policies of
  Council and of the local board of which they are a member.

 The Role of a board member includes:

• Integrating the interests of the Board, community and City.

  Council in accordance with the Board’s protocols.
• Keep the public informed by ensuring that the public knows the status of the
  business of the meeting throughout the meeting.
• Support Board capacity and effectiveness by promoting board member
  participation and development.
• Other roles set out in the Board’s Procedure By-law.
• The Vice-Chair assumes the Chair’s duties when the Chair is not available.

BACKGROUND

Outdoor Education Task Force
At Meeting #6/18 on July 20, 2018, Toronto and Region Conservation Authority’s (TRCA) Board
of Directors approved the establishment of an Outdoor Education Task Force comprised of
Trustees from area school boards and representatives from TRCA’s Board of Directors. The
Outdoor Education Task Force was convened with an eighteen (18) month term and mandate to
study, develop, and recommend strategic future directions related to out-of-classroom learning
as it pertains to natural science, conservation and the environment in the Greater Toronto Area
(GTA), specifically including Peel, York and Durham Regions and the City of Toronto.

TRCA’s Board of Directors convened the Outdoor Education Task Force as a multi-stakeholder
approach to identifying opportunities that will sustain the current system of publicly built and
operated school board and conservation authority out-of-classroom learning centres and
programs into the future.

The Outdoor Education Task Force was comprised of the following School Board Trustees and
TRCA Board members:

      Durham Catholic District School Board: Trustee Morgan Ste. Marie
      York Region District School Board: Trustee Cynthia Cordova
      York Catholic District School Board: Trustee Jennifer Wigston
      Peel District School Board: Trustee Will Davies
      Dufferin-Peel Catholic District School Board: Trustee Frank Di Cosola
      Toronto District School Board: Trustee Anu Sriskandarajah
      Toronto Catholic District School Board: Trustee Garry Tanuan
      Conseil scolaire catholique MonAvenir: Chair Melinda Chartrand
      TRCA (City of Brampton): Regional Councillor Rowena Santos
      TRCA (City of Toronto): Mr. Basu Mukherjee

On January 25, 2021 the Outdoor Education Task Force completed its work and submitted a
Vision Statement and Strategic Recommendations for review and endorsement by TRCA’s
Board of Directors (Attachment #1: Final Report: Vision Statement and Strategic
Recommendations of Outdoor Education Task Force, and Attachment #2: Toronto and Region
Conservation Authority Outdoor Education Task Force Vision Statement). The Outdoor
Education Task Force Vision Statement and Strategic Recommendations form the basis for
strengthened collaboration amongst and between TRCA and area school boards as well as
other learning organizations within the broader public sector. A key goal of the Outdoor
Education Task Force was to build on Section 197 of the Education Act, which provides for
partnerships between school boards and conservation authorities related to natural science and
conservation education activities, and establish mechanisms to better leverage the public
learning assets and natural resources of both school boards and conservation authorities while
maximizing the use of finite financial public and private funding in delivering important nature-
based out-of-classroom learning experiences for students of GTA watersheds and school
boards.
 TRCA’s Board of Directors, at its meeting held on February 26, 2021, adopted Resolution
#A17/21 as follows:

    and recommend strategic future directions related to natural science, conservation and

    Force endorsed the final report, Vision Statement and Strategic Recommendations, as
    amended, for submission to Toronto and Region Conservation Authority Board of Directors;

    THEREFORE, LET IT BE RESOLVED THAT the final report of the Outdoor Education Task
    Force be received;

    Force meeting, be endorsed;

TRCA’s Role in Outdoor Education
TRCA has worked with local schools and school boards to provide outdoor education programs
and services since 1953. Enabling this work, Section 197 of the Education Act provides for
school boards to enter into agreements with conservation authorities for the purposes of
providing out-of-classroom learning related to natural science, conservation or other out-of-
classroom programs. Currently TRCA is one of Ontario’s largest providers of out-of-classroom
experiential learning with over 155,000 students engaging in TRCA learning programs annually
through a network of education centres, conservation areas and local greenspaces, in addition
 to in-school programs. TRCA educational offerings are curriculum-linked and enable student
learning related to a wide range of subjects that meet curricular objectives while advancing
TRCA strategic goals and supporting TRCA’s core mandate.

Further to out-of-classroom learning experiences and program services, TRCA provides access
to TRCA lands and greenspaces for area school boards for board-operated outdoor education
centres through lease or other formal agreements either on, or adjacent, to TRCA-owned land,
thereby maximizing public-sector partnerships through efficient use of publicly owned land for
natural science, conservation and environmental learning purposes.


Natural Science and Education Committee
Central to the Outdoor Education Task Force recommendations was the establishment of the
Natural Science and Education Committee as a standing committee of TRCA’s Board of
Directors to provide a shared governance framework that advances the recommendations of the
Outdoor Education Task Force. TRCA has historically brought key stakeholders together as
necessary for important discussions related to the segment of the formal education system that
relates to natural science, conservation and the environment, most recently through the Outdoor
Education Task Force. The convening of the Natural Science and Education Committee was
seen as an essential component of TRCA’s work as a leader in this field by members of the
Outdoor Education Task Force. To this end, at TRCA’s Board of Directors Meeting held on May
28, 2021, RES.#A107/21 was approved, in part, as follows:

       …THAT the Natural Science and Education Committee be established;

       …THAT a formal request for representation on the Natural Science and Education
       Committee be made to member organizations.

In order to ensure representation from key public-sector stakeholders, membership of the
Natural Science and Education Committee is to be comprised of representatives from the
following:

         (a)   School Board Trustee from each of the area school boards (up to 10);
         (b)   TRCA Board of Directors Member (up to 2);
         (c)   Ministry of Education (up to 2);
         (d)   Indigenous representatives with a Treaty right or historical affiliation to TRCA’s
               jurisdiction (up to 2);
         (e)   Youth representatives (up to 2) attending an educational institution in TRCA’s
               jurisdiction.

Following approval of the establishment of the Natural Science and Education Committee by
TRCA’s Board of Directors, requests for appointment for School Board Trustees were circulated
to area school boards, and a call for applications for Youth Representatives was released. At
TRCA Board of Director’s meeting held on November 19, 2021, the following appointments
were confirmed for the Natural Science and Education Committee:

       School Board Trustees:

       Mr. Stan Cameron, Peel District School Board
       Mr. Nadeem Mahmood, York District School Board
       Mr. Garry Tanuan, Toronto Catholic District School Board
        Ms. Jennifer Wigston, York Catholic District School Board
       Ms. Manna Wong, Toronto District School Board

       Youth Representatives:

       Ms. Alissa Gallizzi
       Mr. Sam Matrosov

       TRCA Board Members:

       Ms. Xiao Han
       Ms. Connie Tang

At the same TRCA Board of Directors meeting, staff were delegated authority to confirm any
further appointments to the Committee, and subsequently, staff received appointments from the
following:

       Mr. Thomas Thomas, Dufferin-Peel District School Board

TRCA staff are continuing to work with indigenous communities and the Ministry of Education to
secure representation on the Natural Science and Education as outlined in the Terms of
Reference and will report back to both TRCA’s Board of Directors and the Natural Science and
Education Committee with updates as appropriate.


RATIONALE
Building on the outcomes and recommendations of the Outdoor Education Task Force, the
Natural Science and Education Committee provides a multi-stakeholder governance framework
to advance shared objectives pertaining to out-of-classroom learning related to natural-science,
conservation and the environment in the Greater Toronto Area. There is currently no formalized
collaborative mechanism to foster, develop and strengthen partnerships between school boards
and conservation authorities to support and enhance student learning in the out-of-doors. By
bringing together key stakeholders, including TRCA, area school boards, the Ministry of
Education, indigenous communities and youth, TRCA and school board partners will be better
able to leverage the value of the publicly built and operated system that supports out-of-
classroom learning related to natural science, conservation and the environment more
effectively, while also ensuring the current and future learning needs are met.

As an advisory board of TRCA’s Board of Directors, the Natural Science and Education
Committee has a mandate to:

       Study and make recommendations to the Board of Directors of TRCA regarding
       recommendations to TRCA and government and agency partners on improvements and
       future needs as it pertains to the provision, planning or access for students to out-of-
       classroom learning related to natural science, conservation and the environment in the
       Greater Toronto Area region.

The objectives of the Natural Science and Education Committee are to advise TRCA and
partner agencies on the effective implementation and advancement of the recommendations of
the Outdoor Education Task Force, specifically the following:
          (a)   Establish Consistent Access and Curricular Standards Across TRCA and School
               Boards.
         (b)   Establish a Unified Performance Measurement System.
         (c)   Advance Shared-Ownership and Access Models That Enhance and Sustain an
               Overall Out-Of-Classroom Learning System.
         (d)   Develop a Long-Term Equitable Access Financial Plan.

To align with municipal and school board election cycles, committee members have been
appointed for the remainder of the municipal council and school board terms. Following the
2022 election cycle, members of the Committee will be appointed for a four-year term aligned
with municipal and school board Terms of Council or until their successors are appointed, with
meetings held, at minimum, three times per year.

2022 Activities and Meeting Formats
Recognizing that municipal and school board elections are scheduled for Monday, October 24,
2022, work related to the current term of the Natural Science and Education Committee will
focus on setting broad objectives for the Natural Science and Education Committee in alignment
with the recommendations of the Outdoor Education Task Force, establishing a Terms of
Reference for a staff working table comprised of representatives from member organizations
and supporting the resumption of out-of-classroom learning during and following the COVID-19
pandemic, as appropriate.

The Natural Science and Education Committee will meet three (3) times in 2022, as outlined
below. The following meeting schedule has been set based on current Board of Trustee and
Municipal Council schedules.

       Monday, February 7, 2022
       Monday, April 4, 2022
       Monday, June 6, 2022

Meetings of the Natural Science and Education Committee will consist of two sessions: a
Governance Session focused on the business and activities of the Committee followed by a
Leadership Session, which functions as a workshop for the Committee to have open
discussions related to the specific actions of the Committee that inform staff reports.
Governance Sessions will be Chaired by a duly elected member of the Natural Science and
Education Committee, while Leadership Sessions will be facilitated either by TRCA staff or
external consultants as required.

As an advisory board of TRCA’s Board of Directors, the Natural Science and Education
Committee will report to TRCA’s Board of Directors with minutes and action items circulated to
participating member organizations as required.


Relationship to Building the Living City, the TRCA 2013-2022 Strategic Plan
This report supports the following strategies set forth in the TRCA 2013-2022 Strategic Plan:
Strategy 3 – Rethink greenspace to maximize its value
Strategy 5 – Foster sustainable citizenship
Strategy 6 – Tell the story of the Toronto region

Subject:     2015 DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS PROPERTY

Date:        2016-03-30


Summary:

This report is intended to update the Board of Management on the disposal of surplus property.

Recommendation:

It is recommended that the Board receive this report for information.

Background:

Throughout the year the Toronto Zoo disposes of items that have been collected through un-
claimed lost and found, and equipment and vehicles that are surplus to the Zoo's needs. Various
items are deemed to be of no value and are donated to charities, are recycled or sent to landfill.
Annually a list of surplus vehicles and/or equipment is prepared for sale or disposal at auction
through Platinum Liquidations and North Toronto Auction, the City's contracted auctioneers.

The proceeds of the sale or auction of items is reported to the Board in accordance with Zoo
Bylaw 2-2010 and the revenue is included in miscellaneous revenues. The net revenue generated
varies each year depending on the number of surplus items as well as the quality of the items sent
to auction.

Comments/Discussion:

In 2015, the Zoo disposed of vehicles and used equipment including items such as snow plows,
sanders and weed eaters.

The net revenue from the sale of surplus property in 2015 was $93,222.00.

Section III – Items for the Information of the Board

TO:           Chair and Members of the Board of Directors
              Friday, May 22, 2026 Meeting
FROM:         Anil Wijesooriya, Director, Restoration and Infrastructure

RE:           LOOP TRAIL UPDATE – MAY 2026

KEY ISSUE
Update on Toronto and Region Conservation Authority’s (TRCA’s)
involvement in the Loop Trail project.

RECOMMENDATION:
WHEREAS the Loop Trail has been identified in the City of Toronto’s
Ravine Strategy as a key initiative supporting the connection of
people to nature and the ravine system;

WHEREAS TRCA has been a supporting partner of the Loop
Trail through a Memorandum of Understanding with the City of
Toronto and Evergreen since 2020;

WHEREAS TRCA is actively working with the City of Toronto
to implement trail projects that close network gaps in support of the
Loop Trail and TRCA’s Trail Strategy for the Greater Toronto Region;
IT IS RECOMMENDED THAT this update and attached presentation on
the TRCA’s involvement in the Loop Trail project be received.

BACKGROUND
The Loop Trail envisions a continuous 72-kilometer multi-use trail around
the City of Toronto combining existing and future trail sections and
connecting communities and amenities. It has been identified by the City of
Toronto’s Ravine Strategy as a key initiative supporting the connection of
people to nature and the ravine system. Components of the Loop Trail
were previously identified in the TRCA Board endorsed Trail Strategy for
the Greater Toronto Region (TRCA Trail Strategy Dashboard). The Loop
Trail project area is generally defined as the Humber River in the west, the
Finch Corridor in the north, the Don River in the east, and the Waterfront in
the south — a geography that forms the namesake ‘loop’. See Attachment
1.
                                                                    Item 9.4
In January 2020 (2020.EX12.1: 9) Toronto City Council authorized the
General Manager, Parks, Forestry and Recreation, in coordination with the
General Manager, Transportation Services, to negotiate and enter into the
appropriate agreements with Evergreen and the TRCA regarding the
advancement of the Loop Trail project.

Since May 2020 TRCA has been engaged in the advancement of the Loop
Trail through a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the City of
Toronto (the “City”) and Evergreen. This MOU has been renewed annually
with the addition of Toronto Foundation as a partner in 2023.

TRCA and the City are in the process of renewing the MOU for an
additional two-year term.
Previous to the Loop Trail concept being advanced, TRCA was already
working with the City to advance elements of the Loop Trail discussed in
later sections of this report.

RATIONALE
The Loop Trail MOU affirms the need for a collaborative governance
structure for the project. This structure is envisioned to carry over into
future phases of the project under subsequent agreements and may be
revisited and updated as needed to reflect the changing needs of the
project at given stages.

The current governance structure defined in the MOU includes a Steering
Committee that provides general oversight of the project. The Committee is
currently composed of representatives from each of the MOU party
organizations (City of Toronto, Evergreen, Toronto Foundation and TRCA).
The Committee meets as needed and attendance is determined by the
meeting agendas. Meetings serve as a forum for members to set
workplans, track progress, provide updates on key project elements, and
seek input on future project deliverables. The Committee is co-chaired by
the City and Evergreen and TRCA has representatives from the
Restoration and Infrastructure Division and the Government and
Community Relations team sitting as members.

In addition to the Steering Committee, the following Advisory Groups are in
place/slated for future establishment:

    Fund Donor Advisors: Donations in support of the project are directed
                                                                   Item 9.4
    to a dedicated fund or funds held at and administered by Toronto
    Foundation. The fund(s) will be established under a separate
    agreement issued by Toronto Foundation, with Evergreen and the
    City signing on as "Donor Advisors";
   Campaign Advisory Group(s): Evergreen and the City are working
    collaboratively to advance early consultation with local philanthropists
    and sector leaders about Toronto’s Ravine Campaign, including the
    Loop Trail. Campaign Advisory groups will be led by the City and
    Evergreen; and
   Community Programming Committee: A Community Programming
    Committee will be established jointly by the City and Evergreen, in
    consultation with the Toronto Foundation to coordinate non-exclusive
    programming in support of the project.

TRCA has been a member of the Loop Trail Steering Committee since
2020 with involvement in Advisory Groups and subcommittees when
appropriate. This role has primarily been supportive, providing expertise to
inform planning, capital improvements, the development of the project
vision and programming priorities.

As a delivery agent, TRCA, in partnership with the City, has been
advancing key trail connections that support the Loop Trail. The following
long-term planning and implementation projects were underway prior to the
Loop Trail initiative being launched and continue to advance under fee for
service agreements with the City.
Mid Humber Gap Trail: This trail gap constitutes a significant barrier to a
continuous multi-use trail system along the Humber River Trail and is a
priority for the future Loop Trail. Located near Weston Road and Lawrence
Avenue West, approximately 800 metres of trail remains to be completed.
TRCA led a Municipal Class Environmental Assessment in partnership with
the City which was approved in December 2023. TRCA is currently
advancing detailed design of the trail with the City of Toronto leading
property related discussions with key stakeholders. For project information
visit: Mid Humber Gap Trail Study – City of Toronto.

East Don Trail: This trail gap is one of the supporting connectors of the
Loop Trail providing a link to the Lower Don Trail and to The Meadoway.
TRCA, in partnership with the City, completed a Municipal Class
Environmental Assessment for the trail which was approved in 2017. The
project is being implemented in phases under Letter Agreement with the
                                                                    Item 9.4
City. Construction for Phase 1 (Lower Don Trail north to The Meadoway)
commenced in 2018 and is currently underway with an estimate completion
by summer 2026. Construction for Phase 2 (Wynford Heights east to
Wigmore Park) commenced in September 2018 and is complete. TRCA is
currently working with a consultant to advance detailed design for Phase 3
(The Meadoway north to Eglinton Avenue East). For project information
visit: East Don Trail Project - Toronto and Region Conservation Authority.

NEXT STEPS
TRCA will continue to support the Loop Trail Steering Committee and
discuss priorities and opportunities to advance the Loop Trail, including
renewal of the existing MoU for another 2-year term. TRCA will also
continue to identify opportunities to advance the Loop Trail as part of
existing and planned works with the City and other agencies so to
coordinate and integrate where feasible and pragmatic, infrastructure asset
maintenance, and trail and restoration projects within the ravine system.
TRCA will work with the City to identify options for a trail connection from
the Loop Trail to the Meadoway, as per Members Motion 2026.IE27.7.

Relationship to TRCA’s 2023-2034 Strategic Plan
This report supports the following Pillar and Outcome set forth in TRCA’s

At TRCA Board of Directors meeting held on April 28, 2023, Resolution RES.#A 77/23
approved updates to TRCA’s Investment Policy. The purpose of this Statement of Policy
and Procedure is to provide guidance over the management of TRCA cash, short-term
and long-term funds. TRCA’s investment objective is to ensure that its financial assets
are invested in a prudent manner and increase the likelihood that such assets will meet
obligations as they come due.
Public Sector Account Standards (PSAS) issued new reporting standard PS 3450
Financial Instruments which changes reporting requirements for certain investments.
TRCA’s Investment Policy included in Attachment 1, has been updated to reflect new
measurement and recognition principals issued by PSAS which is effective for TRCA’s
2023 fiscal year end.
Additionally, at the TRCA Executive Committee meeting held on January 12, 2024, staff
advised the Committee that they would continue to monitor and report on the
environmental impact and sustainability performance of TRCA’s investment portfolio.
The Investment Policy has been updated to formalize this intended reporting.

RATIONALE

PS 3450 Financial Instruments
PS 3450 Financial Instruments, under PSAS became effective for the years
commencing on or after April 1, 2022 and as a result, TRCA is required to follow the
new standards for 2023 fiscal year end reporting. The Investment Policy has been
updated to reflect the new section PS 3450 Financial Instruments, under PSAS. The
                                                                              Item 9.6
new standard requires that investments in equities that are traded in an active market
and derivatives are measured at fair value, with changes recognized in a new financial
statement called the Statement of Remeasurement Gains and Losses. All other
financial instruments are carried at cost or amortized cost. In prior fiscal years, TRCA
reported all investments at cost or amortized cost.
The change in reporting requirements is being implemented prospectively (change is
reported on a go forward basis) and results in minor changes to the accumulated
surplus and net assets reported on the financial statements.

Environmental Impact Assessment
At the January 12, 2024, Executive Committee meeting, staff presented a report on the
environmental impact of TRCA’s investment portfolios. Staff advised the Executive
Committee that they would continue to monitor and report on the environmental impact
of TRCA’s investment portfolio with a goal of continuously improving upon our
sustainability performance. The Investment Policy has been updated to include formal
reporting on environmental impacts and sustainability performance every two years.

This report supports the following Pillar and Outcome set forth in TRCA’s 2023-2034
Strategic Plan:

the Exhibition Place CEO.

Executive Officer, Exhibition Place to investigate the status of the official plan
amendment, as requested by City Council for the grounds of Exhibition Place, report to
the Board with an update in the first quarter of 2018, and invite appropriate City of

along with the attendance by the Chief Planner & Executive Director for the City of
Toronto who responded to questions.
http://app.toronto.ca/tmmis/viewAgendaItemHistory.do?item=2018.EP11.1

from City Planning on the Cultural Heritage Landscape Assessment (CHLA) for
Exhibition Place.
http://app.toronto.ca/tmmis/viewAgendaItemHistory.do?item=2019.EP2.8

At its meeting of May 14, 2019, City Council considered the report Exhibition Place -
Cultural Heritage Landscape Assessment and Next Steps for Master Plan and approved
of several recommendations.
http://app.toronto.ca/tmmis/viewAgendaItemHistory.do?item=2019.TE5.26

COMMENTS

For the information of the Board, the May 14th City report provided a summary of the
Planning Framework for Exhibition Place. In the City of Toronto Official Plan, the
Exhibition Place lands are within the Downtown and Central Waterfront. The lands are
designated as Regeneration Areas and Parks and Open Space Areas.

The Exhibition Place lands are also located within the boundary of the Central
Waterfront Secondary Plan (CWSP) which states that development at Exhibition Place
Exhibition Place Master Plan Development - Status Report
                                                                               Page 3 of 4
 is to respect and celebrate Exhibition Place's existing heritage architecture and views of
heritage buildings from the water. Adaptive re-use of heritage buildings is encouraged.
New development within lands designated Parks and Open Space Areas may only be
considered if existing open space areas are maintained or alternatives to expand the
size and usability of City-owned parks are provided.

Exhibition Place is not regulated by City zoning by-laws but by the City of Toronto Act,
2006. Section 406 of the Act entrusts its management and operations to the Board and
outlines the permitted uses, including parks and exhibition purposes, although it also
provides for the expansion of uses subject to approval of the City.

The Council report indicates that City Planning staff will be undertaking a Master Plan
exercise to provide direction for the future development of Exhibition Place. This Master
Plan exercise was formally launched with a Public Open House on June 25, 2019, with
staff undertaking preliminary analysis and ongoing public and stakeholder engagement.
The Master Plan is intended to be coordinated with the Exhibition Place Strategic Plan
and will consider opportunities to coordinate with the proposed revitalization of Ontario
Place. The anticipated timeframe for completion is the first quarter of 2020. The
elements of the Master Plan study as described in the City report are set out in
Appendix A attached.

COMMENTS

The Board will continue with its annual plan to review key operational process in the
following areas over the next few years:

       2025   Purchasing and Expenditures Review
       2026   Payroll and Benefits Process Controls Review
       2027   Capital Projects Management Process Review
       2028   Parking Process Controls Review

Historically, risk assessment by the City Auditor General Office (AGO) is done every 5
years. The risk assessment process is intended to provide the AGO with a risk ranking
of Exhibition Place relative to other units across other City divisions, agencies, and
corporations.

Event Revenue and Receivables Review 2024                                        Page 2 of 4
 It has been nine (9) years since the Board commenced its first cyclical review of key
business processes. The first process audited was Parking Controls and Parking
Revenue by PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (“PWC”), whom was our auditor of record in
2016. Since then, the Board has engaged the City of Toronto Internal Auditor Office
through a shared services agreement.

For the year ended December 31, 2023, Exhibition Place’s financial statements
reported revenues of $61.8 million. The City Internal Audit Event Services and
Receivables review focused specifically on space rental, show services, and food &
beverage revenue, which amounted to approximately $43.4 million. This review
included the receivables associated with these revenues from Exhibition Place, the
Enercare Centre, and Beanfield Centre.

The report from the City includes:

1) Objectives
2) Review Methodology
3) Findings and Recommendations
4) Management Actions
Objectives of Review
The objectives of this review were to assess whether:

1) Adequate processes and controls were in place for the establishment and
administration of event-related contracts at Exhibition Place, and

2) Any opportunities for improvement to existing processes and controls exist.
Methodology
The review consisted of:

1) Interviews with Exhibition Place staff to obtain an understanding of current
processes and controls in place;

2) A review of policies and procedures;

3) A walkthrough of the Momentus system for bookings pertaining to event contracts;

4) Sample testing of event contracts;

5) Reviews of other documents and records as required;

6) Other auditing procedures as considered necessary.
Findings and Recommendations
City Internal Audit has noted no major issues or weakness in their review. Overall, event
revenues and receivables were recorded accurately and completely.



Event Revenue and Receivables Review 2024                                         Page 3 of 4
 Their review did, however, identify opportunities to further strengthen controls related to
adjustments to rental rates. There were three examples provided in the report.
Managements Response and Action Plan
This is the area where Exhibition Place management provides a response to the audit
recommendation.

Management is receptive to the auditor's suggestions. Staff concur that these instances
are isolated events where the approval was not properly added to the file. To ensure
transparency, consistency, and accuracy of rates offered to clients, staff agree that it is
essential for any adjustments to Board-approved rental rates to be properly documented
and added to the file (Momentus). Moving forward, staff will ensure that proper
documentation, including approvals, is noted in Momentus.

out of construction;
THAT an archaeological investigation be completed, with any
mitigation measures being carried out to the satisfaction of TRCA
staff, at the expense of City of Toronto;
THAT a permit pursuant to the Act and O. Reg 41/24 be obtained prior
to the commencement of construction;
THAT the Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks
(MECP) be notified in accordance with Section 21(6) of the Act;
AND FURTHER THAT authorized TRCA officials be directed to take
the necessary action to finalize the transaction, including obtaining
any necessary approvals and the signing and execution of
documents.

BACKGROUND
City of Toronto has requested a permanent easement on TRCA-owned
lands for lands located south of Horner Street and West of Burlingame
Road, municipally known as 615 Horner Avenue, in the City of Toronto,
required for Toronto Storm Sewer and Outfall Project. The lands were
purchased from Toronto Golf Club on July 25, 1975, under the Etobicoke
Creek Flood Plain Project.
As part of the Basement Flooding Protection Program (BFPP), the City of
Toronto is undertaking projects in several neighbourhoods in Etobicoke
Centre to improve stormwater management and reduce the risk of
basement flooding. These projects involve modifying and upgrading the
storm and sanitary systems and other infrastructure improvements.
City of Toronto is proposing to undertake storm sewer and outfall upgrades
within Etobicoke Valley Park. The proposed work includes a 1200 mm and
1350 mm outfall replacements, stormwater inline storage in large-diameter
circular pipes, sanitary sewer replacement and upgrades, installation of
additional inlet capacity in the form of High-Capacity Inlets (HCIs) and Inlet
control devices (ICDs), and water quality improvements. Open cut trench
excavation method will be used for construction the proposed sewer and
                                                                 Item 9.2
outfall upgrade and the maintenance hole installation.
RATIONALE
Consistent with this long-standing practice and reciprocal municipal
partnership, the City of Toronto has requested that lands required for the
Toronto storm sewer and outfall project be conveyed for nominal
consideration of $10.00. The proposed conveyance supports a municipal
stormwater infrastructure project, aligns with TRCA’s mandate, and reflects
established precedent between the parties. There will be no negative
functional, operational or otherwise material impact on the remainder of
TRCA’s property.

Relationship to TRCA’s 2023-2034 Strategic Plan
This report supports the following Pillar and Outcome set forth in TRCA’s
2023-2034 Strategic Plan:

Pillar 1 Environmental Protection and Hazard Management:
        1.4 Balance development and growth to protect the natural
            environment ensuring safe sustainable development

City of Toronto has agreed to assume all legal, survey and other costs
involved in completing this transaction.

KEY ISSUE

of an Advocacy Agenda designed to raise awareness of the need for

RECOMMENDATION:
WHEREAS NSEC as an advisory committee of Toronto and Region

AND WHEREAS at Meeting #2/23 held on October 11, 2023, NSEC

THEREFORE LET IT BE RESOLVED THAT the following advocacy

and the environment in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) be endorsed.

BACKGROUND

At Meeting #6/18 on July 20, 2018, TRCA Board of Directors approved the
                                                                Item 8.1
establishment of an Outdoor Education Task Force (“Task Force”) with an
eighteen (18) month mandate to study, develop, and recommend strategic
future directions related to out-of-classroom learning related to natural
science, conservation, and the environment in the GTA, specifically
including Peel, York and Durham Regions and the City of Toronto.

Comprised of School Board Trustees and TRCA Board Members, the Task
Force brought forward a series of recommendations intended to strengthen
the overall out-of-classroom learning system. At Meeting #2/21 held on
February 26, 2021, TRCA's Board of Directors endorsed the Final Report
and Recommendations of the Task Force,

     Recommendation #1: Establish Shared Governance Model – Natural
     Science and Education Committee as a Subcommittee of Toronto
     and Region Conservation Authority’s Board of Directors

     Recommendation #2: Establish Consistent Access and Curricular
     Standards Across TRCA and School Boards

     Recommendation #3: Establish a Unified Performance Measurement
     System

     Recommendation #4: Advance Shared-Ownership and Access
     Models That Enhance and Sustain an Overall Out-Of-Classroom
     Learning System

     Recommendation #5: Develop a Long-Term Equitable Access
     Financial Plan

Central to the Task Force recommendations was the establishment of
NSEC as a standing committee of TRCA’s Board of Directors to provide a
shared governance framework that advances the recommendations of the
Task Force. TRCA has historically brought key stakeholders together as
necessary for important discussions related to the segment of the formal
education system that relates to natural science, conservation, and the
environment, most recently through the Task Force. The convening of the
NSEC was seen as an essential component of TRCA’s work as a leader in
this field by members of the Task Force.

At Meeting #3/22 held on June 6, 2022, NSEC endorsed a series of
                                                                Item 8.1
minimum standards for student access to out-of-classroom learning related
to natural science, conservation and the environment. These minimum
standards are intended to form the basis for a cohesive sequential
framework for student access to out-of-classroom learning experiences in
nature. Subsequently, at Meeting #2/23 held on October 11, 2023, NSEC
further received a staff update on the costing model for implementation of
the aforesaid minimum standards and endorsed the following resolutions:


     THEREFORE LET IT BE RESOLVED THAT the information report
     on costing for implementation of minimum standards for access
     to out-of-classroom learning be received;

     THAT TRCA prepare, in consultation with participating school
     boards, appropriate material to support enhanced advocacy
     efforts related to long-term funding for out-of-classroom
     learning in the areas of natural science, conservation and the
     environment;

     AND FURTHER THAT Members of the Natural Science and
     Education Committee continue to advocate for sustained and
     ongoing funding for out-of-classroom learning related to natural
     science, conservation, and the environment.

In order to sustain and ensure the future provision of out-of-classroom
learning for students related to natural science, conservation and the
environment, the Task Force recognized the importance of stable, long-
term funding. This was emphasized in the Final Report of the Task Force,
specifically in Recommendation #5: Develop a Long-Term Equitable
Access Financial Plan.

A key activity of the workplan for NSEC has been to develop a costing of
the implementation of the Minimum Standards for Student Access, as
endorsed at Meeting #3/22 held on June 6, 2022. The following is a budget
framework for each grade covered under the Minimum Standards:

        Recognizing the potential to roll this program out to all students and
